claim: Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to the aorticopulmonary septum.
source: Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to important portions of the cardiovascular system including the aorticopulmonary septum and cardiac ganglion.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known contribution of cardiac neural crest cells.

claim: Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to the cardiac ganglion.
source: Cardiac neural crest cells contribute to important portions of the cardiovascular system including the aorticopulmonary septum and cardiac ganglion.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known contribution of cardiac neural crest cells.

claim: Neural crest cells contribute to cardiomyocytes of the ventricles in Gallus gallus.
source: Using replication incompetent avian retroviruses for precise high-resolution lineage analysis, we uncover a previously undescribed neural crest contribution to cardiomyocytes of the ventricles in Gallus gallus, supported by Wnt1-Cre lineage analysis in Mus musculus.
evidence: The abstract states this finding is based on retroviral lineage analysis experiments performed in the study.

claim: Neural crest cells contribute to cardiomyocytes of the ventricles in Mus musculus.
source: Using replication incompetent avian retroviruses for precise high-resolution lineage analysis, we uncover a previously undescribed neural crest contribution to cardiomyocytes of the ventricles in Gallus gallus, supported by Wnt1-Cre lineage analysis in Mus musculus.
evidence: The abstract states this finding is supported by Wnt1-Cre lineage analysis in mouse.

claim: The adult zebrafish heart has few sox10+ cells in the apex.
source: Whereas the adult heart has few sox10+ cells in the apex, sox10 and other neural crest regulatory network genes are upregulated in the regenerating myocardium after resection.
evidence: This observation is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in the results.

claim: sox10 is upregulated in the regenerating myocardium after resection in zebrafish.
source: Whereas the adult heart has few sox10+ cells in the apex, sox10 and other neural crest regulatory network genes are upregulated in the regenerating myocardium after resection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by in situ hybridization and transgenic reporter data in the results.

claim: Neural crest regulatory network genes are upregulated in the regenerating myocardium after resection in zebrafish.
source: Whereas the adult heart has few sox10+ cells in the apex, sox10 and other neural crest regulatory network genes are upregulated in the regenerating myocardium after resection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptome analysis data in the results.

claim: Neural crest cells contribute to cardiomyocytes across vertebrates.
source: The results suggest that neural crest cells contribute to many cardiovascular structures including cardiomyocytes across vertebrates and to the regenerating heart of teleost fish.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparative data across chick, mouse, and zebrafish presented in the study.

claim: Neural crest cells contribute to the regenerating heart of teleost fish.
source: The results suggest that neural crest cells contribute to many cardiovascular structures including cardiomyocytes across vertebrates and to the regenerating heart of teleost fish.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract based on the zebrafish regeneration experiments.

claim: Removal of the cardiac neural crest results in persistent truncus arteriosus.
source: Ablation studies in chick embryos show that removal of the cardiac crest results in a broad range of defects, including persistent truncus arteriosus, abnormal myocardium function, and misalignment of the arch arteries (Kirby et al., 1983; Waldo et al., 1999; Bockman et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated based on cited ablation studies in chick embryos.

claim: Removal of the cardiac neural crest results in abnormal myocardium function.
source: Ablation studies in chick embryos show that removal of the cardiac crest results in a broad range of defects, including persistent truncus arteriosus, abnormal myocardium function, and misalignment of the arch arteries (Kirby et al., 1983; Waldo et al., 1999; Bockman et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated based on cited ablation studies in chick embryos.

claim: Removal of the cardiac neural crest results in misalignment of the arch arteries.
source: Ablation studies in chick embryos show that removal of the cardiac crest results in a broad range of defects, including persistent truncus arteriosus, abnormal myocardium function, and misalignment of the arch arteries (Kirby et al., 1983; Waldo et al., 1999; Bockman et al., 1987).
evidence: This is stated based on cited ablation studies in chick embryos.

claim: Cardiac neural crest defects are reminiscent of common human congenital heart defects.
source: These defects are highly reminiscent of some of the most common human congenital heart defects.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between experimental defects and human pathology.

claim: Other neural crest populations cannot rescue the effects of cardiac neural crest ablation when grafted in its place.
source: Importantly, other neural crest populations cannot rescue the effects of cardiac neural crest ablation even when grafted in its place, exemplifying the uniqueness of this population (Kirby, 1989).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited study by Kirby, 1989.

claim: The cardiac neural crest is a unique population among neural crest cells.
source: Importantly, other neural crest populations cannot rescue the effects of cardiac neural crest ablation even when grafted in its place, exemplifying the uniqueness of this population (Kirby, 1989).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the inability of other neural crest populations to rescue cardiac neural crest ablation.

claim: Quail-chick transplantation experiments have been used to uncover contributions of the cardiac neural crest to the heart.
source: Classically, quail-chick transplantation experiments have been used to uncover contributions of the cardiac neural crest to the heart, with some more recent attempts using antibody staining of migratory neural crest cells or LacZ retroviral lineage analysis as well as transgenic lines such as Wnt1-Cre driven β-galactosidase in mammals (Kirby et al., 1983; Kuratani and Kirby, 1991; Boot et al., 2003; Jiang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a description of classical methods used in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The cardiac neural crest contributes to smooth muscle cells lining the great arteries.
source: The results suggest that the cardiac neural crest contributes to smooth muscle cells lining the great arteries, outflow tract septum and valves, mesenchyme that remodels pharyngeal arch arteries, and parasympathetic innervation of the heart, such as the cardiac ganglion.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous lineage tracing results from the literature.

claim: The cardiac neural crest contributes to the outflow tract septum and valves.
source: The results suggest that the cardiac neural crest contributes to smooth muscle cells lining the great arteries, outflow tract septum and valves, mesenchyme that remodels pharyngeal arch arteries, and parasympathetic innervation of the heart, such as the cardiac ganglion.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous lineage tracing results from the literature.

claim: The cardiac neural crest contributes to mesenchyme that remodels pharyngeal arch arteries.
source: The results suggest that the cardiac neural crest contributes to smooth muscle cells lining the great arteries, outflow tract septum and valves, mesenchyme that remodels pharyngeal arch arteries, and parasympathetic innervation of the heart, such as the cardiac ganglion.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous lineage tracing results from the literature.

claim: The cardiac neural crest contributes to parasympathetic innervation of the heart.
source: The results suggest that the cardiac neural crest contributes to smooth muscle cells lining the great arteries, outflow tract septum and valves, mesenchyme that remodels pharyngeal arch arteries, and parasympathetic innervation of the heart, such as the cardiac ganglion.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous lineage tracing results from the literature.

claim: Inconsistencies remain between different lineage approaches for cardiac neural crest.
source: However, inconsistencies remain between different lineage approaches, most of which suffer from high background and low cellular resolution.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the current study.

claim: Most previous lineage approaches suffer from high background and low cellular resolution.
source: However, inconsistencies remain between different lineage approaches, most of which suffer from high background and low cellular resolution.
evidence: This is stated as a critique of previous methods.

claim: Neural crest contribution to trabecular myocardium was previously thought to be confined to non-amniotic vertebrates.
source: Using a novel retroviral labeling approach in chick and confirmed by Wnt1-Cre reporter lines in mouse, we reveal a previously undetected contribution of the amniote cardiac neural crest to the trabecular myocardium of the ventricles, a derivative previously thought to be confined to non-amniotic vertebrates (Sato and Yost, 2003; Li et al., 2003; Cavanaugh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge from cited studies in zebrafish.

claim: The adult zebrafish heart exhibits extensive regenerative capacity.
source: As the adult zebrafish heart exhibits extensive regenerative capacity, we turned to this model to test whether the neural crest may contribute to heart regeneration (Poss et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Replication-incompetent avian retrovirus indelibly and precisely marks neural crest progenitors for long term lineage analysis at single cell resolution.
source: To specifically label cardiac neural crest cells prior to their emigration from the neural tube and identify novel progeny of chick cardiac crest, we use a replication-incompetent avian retrovirus (RIA) that indelibly and precisely marks neural crest progenitors for long term lineage analysis at single cell resolution and without the need for tissue grafting.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the method used in the study.

claim: The post-otic neural tube of the hindbrain adjacent to somites 1–3 was injected at HH stage 9–10 with high-titer RIA.
source: To this end, the post-otic neural tube of the hindbrain adjacent to somites 1–3 was injected at Hamburger and Hamilton (HH) stage 9–10 with high-titer (1 × 107 ifu/mL) RIA (Figure 1A), which drives expression of nuclear localized H2B-YFP under control of a constitutive RSV promoter (Li et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2019; Fields-Berry et al., 1992; Chen et al., 1999; Hamburger and Hamilton, 1951).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: At HH stage 9-10, premigratory cardiac neural crest cells are positioned within the dorsal neural tube and about to emigrate.
source: At this stage in the development, premigratory cardiac neural crest cells are positioned within the dorsal neural tube and about to emigrate.
evidence: This is stated as developmental knowledge about the timing of neural crest emigration.

claim: The RIA labeling approach solely marks hindbrain neural tube cells including premigratory cardiac neural crest cells that subsequently delaminate from the dorsal neural tube during a two-hour time window when the virus remains active.
source: Accordingly, this labeling approach solely marks hindbrain neural tube cells including premigratory cardiac neural crest cells that subsequently delaminate from the dorsal neural tube during a two-hour time window when the virus remains active.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the specificity and temporal window of the labeling method.

claim: One day post-infection (HH14), virally labeled progeny are present in the cardiac migration stream en route to pharyngeal arch 3.
source: One day after injection, whole mount imaging revealed RIA-labeled cells migrating in a stream along pharyngeal arch 3 (Figure 1B,B'), that subsequently accumulated in pharyngeal arches 3, 4 and 6 two days after infection (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Two days post-infection, virally labeled cardiac crest cells accumulated in pharyngeal arches 3, 4 and 6.
source: One day after injection, whole mount imaging revealed RIA-labeled cells migrating in a stream along pharyngeal arch 3 (Figure 1B,B'), that subsequently accumulated in pharyngeal arches 3, 4 and 6 two days after infection (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: All labeled cells in the periphery co-localized with the migratory neural crest marker, HNK-1.
source: Next, we confirmed that all labeled cells in the periphery co-localized with the migratory neural crest marker, HNK-1, demonstrating that the neural crest is the only population labeled with H2B-YFP outside the neural tube, thus verifying specificity of infection (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The neural crest is the only population labeled with H2B-YFP outside the neural tube.
source: Next, we confirmed that all labeled cells in the periphery co-localized with the migratory neural crest marker, HNK-1, demonstrating that the neural crest is the only population labeled with H2B-YFP outside the neural tube, thus verifying specificity of infection (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the HNK-1 co-localization experiment.

claim: Labeled cardiac crest cells populate the cardiovascular system in a proximal to distal progression.
source: With time, labeled cardiac crest cells were observed in numerous and diverse derivatives, populating the cardiovascular system in a proximal to distal progression (Figure 1E–I, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E-I and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: RIA-labeled cells were observed adjacent to and within the walls of pharyngeal arch arteries.
source: Consistent with quail-chick chimera, we observed RIA-labeled cells adjacent to and within the walls of pharyngeal arch arteries, in the aorticopulmonary septum, outflow tract, and cardiac cushion.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the retroviral labeling experiments.

claim: RIA-labeled cells were observed in the aorticopulmonary septum.
source: Consistent with quail-chick chimera, we observed RIA-labeled cells adjacent to and within the walls of pharyngeal arch arteries, in the aorticopulmonary septum, outflow tract, and cardiac cushion.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the retroviral labeling experiments.

claim: RIA-labeled cells were observed in the outflow tract.
source: Consistent with quail-chick chimera, we observed RIA-labeled cells adjacent to and within the walls of pharyngeal arch arteries, in the aorticopulmonary septum, outflow tract, and cardiac cushion.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the retroviral labeling experiments.

claim: RIA-labeled cells were observed in the cardiac cushion.
source: Consistent with quail-chick chimera, we observed RIA-labeled cells adjacent to and within the walls of pharyngeal arch arteries, in the aorticopulmonary septum, outflow tract, and cardiac cushion.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the retroviral labeling experiments.

claim: YFP-labeled cells were observed in the superior interventricular septum.
source: Moreover, we definitively observed YFP-labeled cells in the superior interventricular septum, a site for which the neural crest contribution has been controversial, although ventricular septal defects are common after cardiac neural crest ablation (Kirby et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated as a novel observation from the retroviral labeling experiments.

claim: The neural crest contribution to the superior interventricular septum has been controversial.
source: Moreover, we definitively observed YFP-labeled cells in the superior interventricular septum, a site for which the neural crest contribution has been controversial, although ventricular septal defects are common after cardiac neural crest ablation (Kirby et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about the controversy in the field.

claim: Ventricular septal defects are common after cardiac neural crest ablation.
source: Moreover, we definitively observed YFP-labeled cells in the superior interventricular septum, a site for which the neural crest contribution has been controversial, although ventricular septal defects are common after cardiac neural crest ablation (Kirby et al., 1985).
evidence: This is stated based on a cited study by Kirby et al., 1985.

claim: Cells of the outflow tract septum and pharyngeal arch arteries differentiated into smooth muscle actin (SMA) positive cells on embryonic day (E) 5.
source: The cells of the outflow tract septum and pharyngeal arch arteries differentiated into smooth muscle actin (SMA) positive cells on embryonic day (E) 5 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: By E3 and onward, virally labeled neural crest cells were observed in the myocardium of both the outflow tract and the ventricles.
source: Importantly, by E3 and onward, virally labeled neural crest cells were observed in the myocardium of both the outflow tract and the ventricles, where they expressed the myocardial markers, Troponin T and Myosin Heavy Chain (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, outflow tract; Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, ventricles).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Virally labeled neural crest cells in the myocardium expressed the myocardial markers, Troponin T and Myosin Heavy Chain.
source: Importantly, by E3 and onward, virally labeled neural crest cells were observed in the myocardium of both the outflow tract and the ventricles, where they expressed the myocardial markers, Troponin T and Myosin Heavy Chain (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, outflow tract; Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, ventricles).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes were not actively undergoing cell division.
source: These neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes were not actively undergoing cell division or programmed cell death (Figure 2E,F), consistent with the stable presence of cells observed over time (Figure 1I, Supplementary file 1a,1b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E with phosphohistone H3 staining.

claim: Neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes were not undergoing programmed cell death.
source: These neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes were not actively undergoing cell division or programmed cell death (Figure 2E,F), consistent with the stable presence of cells observed over time (Figure 1I, Supplementary file 1a,1b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2F with Caspase 3 staining.

claim: Previous lineage tracing experiments in zebrafish showed that a stream of neural crest cells integrate into the myocardium of the primitive heart tube to give rise to cardiomyocytes.
source: While previous lineage tracing experiments in zebrafish showed that a stream of neural crest cells integrate into the myocardium of the primitive heart tube to give rise to cardiomyocytes, our results present the first evidence of a homologous neural crest contribution to cardiomyocytes in chick embryos (Sato and Yost, 2003; Li et al., 2003; Cavanaugh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge from cited zebrafish studies.

claim: The current results present the first evidence of a homologous neural crest contribution to cardiomyocytes in chick embryos.
source: While previous lineage tracing experiments in zebrafish showed that a stream of neural crest cells integrate into the myocardium of the primitive heart tube to give rise to cardiomyocytes, our results present the first evidence of a homologous neural crest contribution to cardiomyocytes in chick embryos (Sato and Yost, 2003; Li et al., 2003; Cavanaugh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: In Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreenfl/fl transgenic mice, neural crest cells are labeled with cytoplasmic GFP.
source: To test whether the contribution of cardiac neural crest cells to the myocardium was conserved in mammals, we examined Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreenfl/fl transgenic mice in which neural crest cells were labeled with cytoplasmic GFP (Chai et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the mouse transgenic line used.

claim: A large number of ZsGreen-positive myocardial cells were observed in the outflow tract and ventricles of E15.5 Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreenfl/fl mouse embryos.
source: Analogous to the results in chick embryos, we observed a large number of ZsGreen-positive myocardial cells in the outflow tract and ventricles, as confirmed by Troponin T expression (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreenfl/fl transgenic line has been associated with ectopic expression due to endogenous Wnt1 activation caused by in-frame ATG located upstream of Wnt1 start codon.
source: To avoid ectopic expression that has been associated with the Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreenfl/fl transgenic line due to endogenous Wnt1 activation caused by in-frame ATG located upstream of Wnt1 start codon, we tested an improved Wnt1 line (Wnt1-Cre2+; R26mTmG mouse line) without ectopic activation of canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway (Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a known issue with the original Wnt1-Cre line, supported by a citation.

claim: The Wnt1-Cre2+; R26mTmG mouse line does not have ectopic activation of canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway.
source: To avoid ectopic expression that has been associated with the Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreenfl/fl transgenic line due to endogenous Wnt1 activation caused by in-frame ATG located upstream of Wnt1 start codon, we tested an improved Wnt1 line (Wnt1-Cre2+; R26mTmG mouse line) without ectopic activation of canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway (Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the improved Wnt1 line, supported by a citation.

claim: Results from the Wnt1-Cre2+; R26mTmG mouse line were similar to those observed with the Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreenfl/fl transgenic mice.
source: The results were similar to those observed with the Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreenfl/fl transgenic mice (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: In mouse embryos, neural crest derived cells were present in the outflow tract, interventricular septum, and myocardium of both ventricles.
source: As in the chick embryos, murine neural crest derived cells were present in the outflow tract, interventricular septum, and myocardium of both ventricles.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the mouse lineage tracing results.

claim: The numbers of neural crest-derived cells appear to decrease with distance along the proximal-to-distal axis in mouse hearts.
source: The numbers of neural crest-derived cells appear to decrease with distance along the proximal-to-distal axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), such that no neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes were observed in the apex of the heart (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, D, E.

claim: No neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes were observed in the apex of the mouse heart.
source: The numbers of neural crest-derived cells appear to decrease with distance along the proximal-to-distal axis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), such that no neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes were observed in the apex of the heart (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: In mouse, the numbers of Wnt1+ cells remain stable with time.
source: As in the chick, the numbers of Wnt1+ cells remain stable with time, and the cells do not appear to undergo active cell division or apoptosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,B',C,C').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,B',C,C'.

claim: Wnt1+ cells in mouse hearts do not appear to undergo active cell division or apoptosis.
source: As in the chick, the numbers of Wnt1+ cells remain stable with time, and the cells do not appear to undergo active cell division or apoptosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,B',C,C').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,B',C,C'.

claim: The cardiac crest contribution persists postnatally, as Wnt1+ cells are present at postnatal day 2.
source: This contribution persists postnatally, as Wnt1+ cells are present at postnatal day 2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-H.

claim: The results are consistent with previous studies using less specific P0-cre lines.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies using less specific P0-cre lines and demonstrate that comparable cardiac crest contributions occur in birds and mammals (Tomita et al., 2005; Tamura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Comparable cardiac crest contributions occur in birds and mammals.
source: These results are consistent with previous studies using less specific P0-cre lines and demonstrate that comparable cardiac crest contributions occur in birds and mammals (Tomita et al., 2005; Tamura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative data in chick and mouse.

claim: Neural crest lineage labeled cells represent approximately 17% of the population in the proximal half of the mouse ventricle.
source: Quantification of numbers of neural crest lineage labeled cells in the trabeculated myocardium of mice reveals that they represent approximately 17% of the population in the proximal half of the ventricle (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a quantification result from the mouse experiments.

claim: The lineage contributions of neural crest-derived cells in chick and mouse are remarkably similar to those previously shown in zebrafish.
source: The lineage contributions of neural crest-derived cells in chick and mouse are remarkably similar to those previously shown in zebrafish (Sato and Yost, 2003; Li et al., 2003; Cavanaugh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison across species, supported by citations.

claim: In all three species (chick, mouse, zebrafish), neural crest cells contribute to cardiomyocytes of the trabecular myocardium.
source: In all three species, neural crest cells contribute to cardiomyocytes of the trabecular myocardium.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the comparative findings across species.

claim: In adult birds and mammals, cardiac injury leads to scarring with little regeneration.
source: In adult birds and mammals, cardiac injury leads to scarring with little regeneration, whereas heart regeneration is common in amphibians and fish (González-Rosa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Heart regeneration is common in amphibians and fish.
source: In adult birds and mammals, cardiac injury leads to scarring with little regeneration, whereas heart regeneration is common in amphibians and fish (González-Rosa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Adult zebrafish have the capacity to regenerate their hearts after removal of up to 20% of the ventricle.
source: For example, adult zebrafish have the capacity to regenerate their hearts after removal of up to 20% of the ventricle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about zebrafish heart regeneration.

claim: Zebrafish heart regeneration occurs by dedifferentiation and proliferation of pre-existing cardiomyocytes.
source: This has been shown to occur by dedifferentiation and proliferation of pre-existing cardiomyocytes (Poss et al., 2002; Jopling et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Cardiac neural crest cells give rise to a portion of zebrafish cardiomyocytes during development.
source: Given that cardiac neural crest cells give rise to a portion of zebrafish cardiomyocytes during development (Sato and Yost, 2003; Li et al., 2003; Cavanaugh et al., 2015) similar to those we report here in chick and mouse, we next asked whether the progeny of these cells might have the ability to contribute to heart regeneration in adult zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: Tg(−4.9sox10:eGFP) labels all embryonic migratory neural crest lineages.
source: To address this possibility, we first turned to a transgenic line expressing GFP under the control of a sox10 promoter, Tg(−4.9sox10:eGFP), that labels all embryonic migratory neural crest lineages to address whether neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes reactivated their developmental program upon injury (Carney et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the transgenic line used, supported by a citation.

claim: sox10 is expressed in migrating zebrafish cardiac neural crest cells.
source: While sox10 is expressed in migrating zebrafish cardiac neural crest cells, it is down-regulated in the embryo shortly after these cells reach the heart (Cavanaugh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: sox10 is down-regulated in the embryo shortly after neural crest cells reach the heart.
source: While sox10 is expressed in migrating zebrafish cardiac neural crest cells, it is down-regulated in the embryo shortly after these cells reach the heart (Cavanaugh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by a citation.

claim: Very few cells within the apex of the adult myocardium of control adult fish expressed sox10 one month post-sham injury.
source: We confirmed this in adult hearts, finding that very few cells within the apex of the adult myocardium of control adult fish expressed sox10 one month post-sham injury, in which the body cavity was opened but no resection was made (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 1c, n = 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: After surgical removal of ~20% of the ventricular apex, cells in the heart reactivated the sox10 promotor sequence and began to re-express GFP in cardiomyocytes of the trabeculated myocardium near the injured site by 7 days post resection.
source: However, after surgical removal of ~20% of the ventricular apex, cells in the heart reactivated the sox10 promotor sequence and began to re-express GFP in cardiomyocytes of the trabeculated myocardium near the injured site by 7 days post resection (dpa) (Figure 4A; n = 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GFP expression after injury was not limited to the regenerating tissue but was also observed in the uninjured part of the ventricle.
source: GFP expression was not limited to the regenerating tissue but was also observed in the uninjured part of the ventricle.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the regeneration experiments.

claim: By 21dpa, the hearts had undergone vast regeneration and morphologically were nearly indistinguishable from controls.
source: By 21dpa, the hearts had undergone vast regeneration and morphologically were nearly indistinguishable from controls (Figure 4A; n = 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The regenerating apex was comprised of more sox10+ positive cells.
source: Interestingly, consistent with our prediction, the regenerating apex was comprised of more sox10+ positive cells (Figure 4A,B, Supplementary file 1c), suggesting that these cells had proliferated and redeployed a neural crest gene regulatory program during the heart regeneration process.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A,B and Supplementary file 1c.

claim: sox10+ cells had proliferated and redeployed a neural crest gene regulatory program during the heart regeneration process.
source: Interestingly, consistent with our prediction, the regenerating apex was comprised of more sox10+ positive cells (Figure 4A,B, Supplementary file 1c), suggesting that these cells had proliferated and redeployed a neural crest gene regulatory program during the heart regeneration process.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation of increased sox10+ cells in the regenerating apex.

claim: Endogenous sox10 mRNA expression was observed in uninjured, 7dpa, and 21dpa hearts by paraffin section in situ hybridization.
source: To test if sox10 and other bona fide neural crest markers such as tfap2a, were upregulated endogenously, we performed in situ hybridization on paraffin sections of regenerating and uninjured ventricles. The results reveal upregulation of expression of sox10 and tfap2a transcripts after injury, whereas they were mostly absent from uninjured ventricles (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: sox10 transcripts are upregulated after injury in zebrafish hearts.
source: To test if sox10 and other bona fide neural crest markers such as tfap2a, were upregulated endogenously, we performed in situ hybridization on paraffin sections of regenerating and uninjured ventricles. The results reveal upregulation of expression of sox10 and tfap2a transcripts after injury, whereas they were mostly absent from uninjured ventricles (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: tfap2a transcripts are upregulated after injury in zebrafish hearts.
source: To test if sox10 and other bona fide neural crest markers such as tfap2a, were upregulated endogenously, we performed in situ hybridization on paraffin sections of regenerating and uninjured ventricles. The results reveal upregulation of expression of sox10 and tfap2a transcripts after injury, whereas they were mostly absent from uninjured ventricles (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: sox10 and tfap2a transcripts were mostly absent from uninjured ventricles.
source: To test if sox10 and other bona fide neural crest markers such as tfap2a, were upregulated endogenously, we performed in situ hybridization on paraffin sections of regenerating and uninjured ventricles. The results reveal upregulation of expression of sox10 and tfap2a transcripts after injury, whereas they were mostly absent from uninjured ventricles (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: sox10 transcripts co-localize with Tg(sox10:GAL4-UAS-Cre;ubi-Switch) labeled cells.
source: Furthermore, we observed co-localization of sox10 transcripts with a Tg(sox10:GAL4-UAS-Cre;ubi-Switch), which permanently labels all sox10-derived lineages with mCherry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, n = 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tg(sox10:GAL4-UAS-Cre;ubi-Switch) permanently labels all sox10-derived lineages with mCherry.
source: Furthermore, we observed co-localization of sox10 transcripts with a Tg(sox10:GAL4-UAS-Cre;ubi-Switch), which permanently labels all sox10-derived lineages with mCherry (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, n = 2). The Tg(sox10:GAL4-UAS-Cre;ubi-Switch) is a double transgenic line for the sox10:GAL4-UAS-Cre transgene and the ubi:Switch reporter in which the sox10 promoter drives expression of Cre recombinase. Upon activation of sox10 expression in neural crest cells, eGFP is excised and so cells of the sox10 lineage are permanently labeled with mCherry (Cavanaugh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the transgenic line, supported by a citation.

claim: All cells expressing sox10+ transcripts also had mCherry in the Tg(sox10:GAL4-UAS-Cre;ubi-Switch) line.
source: All cells expressing sox10+ transcripts also had mCherry, though not all mCherry positive cells were sox10+ at the 7 day time point (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, insets 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Not all mCherry positive cells were sox10+ at the 7 day time point.
source: All cells expressing sox10+ transcripts also had mCherry, though not all mCherry positive cells were sox10+ at the 7 day time point (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, insets 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ablation of the embryonic neural crest yields few or no sox10+ cells in the adult heart and results in severe heart defects.
source: Our results are consistent with recent findings from Abdul-Wajid and colleagues, who observed that ablation of the embryonic neural crest yields few or no sox10+ cells in the adult heart and results in severe heart defects (Abdul-Wajid et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study by Abdul-Wajid et al., 2018.

claim: There are no subsequent post-embryonic neural crest additions to the heart.
source: This suggests there are no subsequent post-embryonic neural crest additions to the heart and that the population we observe re-expressing neural crest genes are embryonic-derived neural crest progeny.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the ablation study results.

claim: The population re-expressing neural crest genes are embryonic-derived neural crest progeny.
source: This suggests there are no subsequent post-embryonic neural crest additions to the heart and that the population we observe re-expressing neural crest genes are embryonic-derived neural crest progeny.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the lineage tracing and ablation data.

claim: The neural crest developmental gene regulatory network is being redeployed in neural crest-derived cells of the heart during regeneration.
source: These results raise the intriguing possibility that the neural crest developmental gene regulatory network was being redeployed in neural crest-derived cells of the heart during regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the observation of neural crest gene upregulation during regeneration.

claim: 1093 genes are significantly enriched (p-adj <0.05) in regenerating sox10+ cells compared to sox10- cells of the same injured ventricles.
source: This led to the identification of 1093 genes that are significantly enriched (p-adj <0.05) in regenerating sox10+ cells compared to sox10- cells of the same injured ventricles (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a result from the transcriptome analysis and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Many genes of the embryonic neural crest gene regulatory network are upregulated at the time of regeneration.
source: We then compared the differentially expressed genes of isolated 21dpa sox10+ cells to: 1) our recently published chick developmental cardiac neural crest gene regulatory program, 2) known zebrafish neural crest genes, and 3) core neural crest gene regulatory network genes expressed at all axial levels (Tani-Matsuhana et al., 2018; Martik and Bronner, 2017; Lukoseviciute et al., 2018). The results revealed upregulation of many genes of the embryonic neural crest gene regulatory network at the time of regeneration (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Numerous genes known to be responsible for cardiomyocyte proliferation are expressed in sox10+ cells upon heart injury.
source: Interestingly, numerous genes known to be responsible for cardiomyocyte proliferation also are expressed in sox10+ cells upon heart injury (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E) (González-Rosa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: There is an upregulation of a cell proliferation gene signature in sox10+ cells.
source: The co-expression of these genes as well as an upregulation of a cell proliferation gene signature suggests a role for sox10-derived cells in cardiomyocyte proliferation during regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: sox10-derived cells have a role in cardiomyocyte proliferation during regeneration.
source: The co-expression of these genes as well as an upregulation of a cell proliferation gene signature suggests a role for sox10-derived cells in cardiomyocyte proliferation during regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the gene expression data.

claim: The population of proliferating cardiomyocytes in the regenerating heart is heterogeneous and comprised of both neural crest- and mesoderm-derived cardiomyocytes.
source: Furthermore, these results suggest that the population of proliferating cardiomyocytes in the regenerating heart is heterogeneous and comprised of both neural crest- and mesoderm-derived cardiomyocytes (González-Rosa et al., 2017; Sánchez-Iranzo et al., 2018; Schindler et al., 2014; Kikuchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the current results and cited literature.

claim: Neural crest-derived cells (progenitors and/or pre-existing cardiomyocytes) may represent a key population that proliferates and differentiates into new cardiomyocytes after injury.
source: Based on our observation on the lineage relationship between cardiac neural crest cells and cardiomyocytes during development, we propose that neural crest-derived cells (progenitors and/or pre-existing cardiomyocytes) may represent a key population that proliferates and differentiates into new cardiomyocytes after injury.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on the developmental and regeneration data.

claim: The cell lineage labeling results provide direct evidence for a neural crest contribution to the undamaged myocardium of the amniote heart.
source: Our cell lineage labeling results provide direct evidence for a neural crest contribution to the undamaged myocardium of the amniote heart.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings from the chick and mouse experiments.

claim: After injury, there is activation of numerous neural crest gene regulatory transcription factors and other neural crest genes during regeneration.
source: Furthermore, consistent with previous lineage tracing experiments in zebrafish (Cavanaugh et al., 2015), where a proportion of cardiac crest derived-cells were located in the trabeculated myocardium in adult fish, we show that after injury, there is activation of numerous neural crest gene regulatory transcription factors and other neural crest genes during regeneration (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the zebrafish regeneration experiments and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The underlying gene regulatory network of neural crest cells is responsible for formation of cardiomyocytes during normal development.
source: While the underlying gene regulatory network of neural crest cells is responsible for formation of cardiomyocytes during normal development, we speculate that it also does so in a similar manner upon injury by redeploying sox10 and other neural crest gene regulatory network genes.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the developmental and regeneration data.

claim: The neural crest gene regulatory network may function in a similar manner upon injury by redeploying sox10 and other neural crest gene regulatory network genes.
source: While the underlying gene regulatory network of neural crest cells is responsible for formation of cardiomyocytes during normal development, we speculate that it also does so in a similar manner upon injury by redeploying sox10 and other neural crest gene regulatory network genes.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the observation of neural crest gene reactivation during regeneration.

claim: sox10-derived cells are primarily in the proximal trabecular myocardium of the zebrafish heart.
source: The finding that sox10-derived cells are primarily in the proximal trabecular myocardium of the zebrafish heart suggests that these cells must be migrating into to the wound site after injury.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the zebrafish experiments.

claim: sox10-derived cells must be migrating into the wound site after injury.
source: The finding that sox10-derived cells are primarily in the proximal trabecular myocardium of the zebrafish heart suggests that these cells must be migrating into to the wound site after injury.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the spatial distribution of sox10+ cells.

claim: The cells that reactivate sox10 and the neural crest program may come from another adult lineage.
source: Of course, we cannot rule out the possibility that the cells that reactivate sox10 and the neural crest program may come from another adult lineage.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative possibility that cannot be ruled out.

claim: In the adult, the molecular signature of sox10+ cells strongly correlates with that of embryonic neural crest cells.
source: But in the adult, their molecular signature strongly correlates with that of embryonic neural crest cells (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the transcriptome analysis and shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: The sox10+ cells contribute to cardiomyocytes.
source: Whereas our data clearly show that the sox10+ cells contribute to cardiomyocytes (Figure 4A), whether they also might contribute to other lineages (e.g. hematopoietic cells) within the regenerated tissue remains to be explored.
evidence: This is stated as a clear finding from the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Whether sox10+ cells might contribute to other lineages (e.g. hematopoietic cells) within the regenerated tissue remains to be explored.
source: Whereas our data clearly show that the sox10+ cells contribute to cardiomyocytes (Figure 4A), whether they also might contribute to other lineages (e.g. hematopoietic cells) within the regenerated tissue remains to be explored.
evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claim: Quail-chick chimera are generated via transplantation of donor tissue into the host, which requires time to heal.
source: Interspecific quail-chick chimera are generated via transplantation of donor tissue into the host, which requires time to heal (Kirby et al., 1983).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the quail-chick chimera method, supported by a citation.

claim: If the neural crest cells that migrate to the ventricles are the earliest migrating cells, this population may have been delayed after grafting due to wound healing and hence unable to migrate as far.
source: If the neural crest cells that migrate to the ventricles are the earliest migrating cells, this population may have been delayed after grafting due to wound healing and hence unable to migrate as far.
evidence: This is stated as a possible explanation for why the contribution was missed in previous studies.

claim: The labeled cells may have been missed since it can be challenging to identify a small population of dispersed quail cells amongst many more numerous chick cells.
source: Alternatively, the labeled cells may have been missed since it can be challenging to identify a small population of dispersed quail cells amongst many more numerous chick cells.
evidence: This is stated as another possible explanation for why the contribution was missed in previous studies.

claim: Cell behavior might be altered when transplanted quail cells are introduced into a chick environment.
source: Furthermore, cell behavior might be altered when transplanted quail cells are introduced into a chick environment.
evidence: This is stated as a potential confounding factor in quail-chick chimera experiments.

claim: Retroviral lineage labeling circumvents issues of quail-chick chimera by indelibly labeling an endogenous neural crest population without the need for grafting.
source: Our retroviral lineage labeling circumvents these issues by indelibly labeling an endogenous neural crest population without the need for grafting.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the retroviral method over quail-chick chimera.

claim: The labeled cells are easily detectable due to their fluorescent readout.
source: Moreover, the labeled cells are easily detectable due to their fluorescent readout.
evidence: This is stated as another advantage of the retroviral method.

claim: There were hints in the literature regarding a possible neural crest contribution to cardiomyocytes in mice.
source: For lineage labeling in mice, there were hints in the literature regarding a possible neural crest contribution to cardiomyocytes.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge about previous mouse studies.

claim: Previous experiments in mice were either indirect or used lineage tracing techniques that were not specific to the neural crest.
source: However, the experiments were either indirect or used lineage tracing techniques that were not specific to the neural crest.
evidence: This is stated as a critique of previous mouse studies.

claim: Cells isolated from 'cardiospheres' can behave like neural crest cells when injected into chick embryos.
source: For example, Tomita et al. showed that cells isolated from 'cardiospheres' can behave like neural crest cells when injected into chick embryos (Tomita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study by Tomita et al., 2005.

claim: Lineage analysis in mouse using a P0-cre line revealed EGFP-positive cells in the myocardium that gather at the ischemic border upon injury.
source: In addition, lineage analysis in mouse using a P0-cre line revealed EGFP-positive cells in the myocardium that gather at the ischemic border upon injury (Tomita et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a cited study by Tomita et al., 2005.

claim: P0 is not a neural crest specific marker.
source: However, P0 is not a neural crest specific marker, making these results inconclusive at the time.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the P0-cre lineage tracing approach.

claim: Wnt1 is the 'gold standard' for neural crest labeling.
source: In contrast, Wnt1 is the 'gold standard' for neural crest labeling and the improved Wnt1 line (Wnt1-Cre2+; R26mTmG) corrects possible ectopic expression problematic in the original Wnt1-Cre;ZsGreen line (Jiang et al., 2000; Chai et al., 2000; Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Wnt1 as a neural crest marker, supported by citations.

claim: In chick and mouse, neural crest-derived cells comprise a significant portion (~17%) of the trabeculated myocardium in the proximal part of both ventricles.
source: In chick and mouse, neural crest-derived cells comprise a significant portion (~17%) of the trabeculated myocardium in the proximal part of both ventricles.
evidence: This is stated as a quantification result from the chick and mouse experiments.

claim: The percentage of neural crest-derived cells in amniotes is similar to what has been reported in zebrafish.
source: Interestingly, this percentage is similar to what has been reported in zebrafish (Cavanaugh et al., 2015; Abdul-Wajid et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison with cited zebrafish studies.

claim: In amniotes, the density of neural crest-derived cells decreases along the proximal-distal axis and appears to be stable through time.
source: In amniotes, we find that the density of the cells decreases along the proximal-distal axis and appears to be stable through time (Figure 1I, Supplementary file 1a,b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1I and Supplementary file 1a,b.

claim: The presence of neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes across vertebrates and the redeployment of a sox10+ cell population in zebrafish heart regeneration suggest that the neural crest-derived myocardium might also play a role in heart regeneration in neonatal mice.
source: The presence of neural crest-derived cardiomyocytes across vertebrates and the redeployment of a sox10+ cell population in zebrafish heart regeneration suggest that the neural crest-derived myocardium might also play a role in heart regeneration in neonatal mice, which requires further testing.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the comparative findings across species.

claim: The mechanisms that control the normal development of the neural crest into cardiomyocytes may be harnessed to stimulate these cells to proliferate and regenerate new cardiomyocytes.
source: If the results extrapolate to other species, the mechanisms that control the normal development of the neural crest into cardiomyocytes may be harnessed to stimulate these cells to proliferate and regenerate new cardiomyocytes, thus offering potential therapeutic approaches to repair heart damage in mammals including humans.
evidence: This is stated as a potential therapeutic implication of the findings.

claim: Understanding neural crest development into cardiomyocytes may offer potential therapeutic approaches to repair heart damage in mammals including humans.
source: If the results extrapolate to other species, the mechanisms that control the normal development of the neural crest into cardiomyocytes may be harnessed to stimulate these cells to proliferate and regenerate new cardiomyocytes, thus offering potential therapeutic approaches to repair heart damage in mammals including humans.
evidence: This is stated as a potential therapeutic implication of the findings.
